questions.q: According to this lesson, what are the four things executives actually listen for in a presentation like this?
options: A full reading of the Lesson 16 strategy document section by section
Time compressed to seconds, risk stated in dollars, a roadmap that reads as momentum, and one specific ask
A detailed list of every SQL query written across the program
Nothing specific — any format works equally well for a board
questions.explain: The lesson names exactly these four things as what a board listens for, contrasted with a practitioner's instinct to lead with technical detail.

questions.q: What is the 'hook' that opens the presentation, and why that choice?
options: A summary of Lesson 12's operating model, because it's the most recently built deliverable
The same GDPR incident from Lesson 1 — a six-week DSAR and conflicting order histories — because it already reached the board once and the room half-remembers it
A technical walkthrough of the Snowflake schema
An unrelated industry statistic about data breaches
questions.explain: The lesson explains the presentation opens with the same incident from Lesson 1 specifically because it's already familiar to the audience, making the eventual ask land as finishing known work.

questions.q: How does this lesson frame regulatory risk for the board, instead of using governance jargon?
options: By citing UK GDPR's real penalty structure — up to 4% of global annual turnover or £17.5 million, whichever is greater — as context for the exposure
By inventing a specific dollar fine LTV Global will definitely pay
By avoiding any mention of financial or regulatory consequences
By comparing LTV Global to a real named company that was fined
questions.explain: The lesson uses the real, public UK GDPR penalty ceiling as context for risk framing, explicitly not as a specific prediction, and is careful to note this fact is real while LTV Global itself is fictional.

questions.q: What three things make up 'the ask' at the end of the presentation?
options: A request for a new company logo, an email signature, and a new meeting room
A request to cancel the governance program entirely
Funding to build the Lesson 14 architecture in production, headcount for the governance office, and renewal of Dana Whitfield's mandate
A request for Marcus Ibe to be replaced
questions.explain: The lesson specifies these three concrete, decidable items as the presentation's closing ask.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say 'What we built' should be stated as four outcomes rather than fourteen lesson titles?
options: Because fourteen titles would take too long to design as slides
Because a board responds to outcomes (owners named, one golden record, governed AI, a real architecture), not an inventory of internal deliverable names
Because only four lessons actually produced anything useful
Because the board already read all fourteen files beforehand
questions.explain: The lesson explains that compressing fourteen lesson-level deliverables into four outcome statements communicates impact to a non-specialist audience far better than a deliverable-by-deliverable list.
